newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices soar, grains fall on weather.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices soar, grains fall on weather.

text.p: Gasoline prices ended sharply higher on Friday as oil traders continued to worry about supplies of crude oil and refined products going into winter.
Gasoline for October delivery settled up 1.61 cents to 64.60 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Heating oil prices have risen more than 25 percent in the last three months as weekly data on stocks showed supplies well below those of a year ago and little buildup of stocks.
Heating oil's price gains have also buoyed crude oil but gasoline prices have lagged, one reason for the speculative buying on Friday, analysts said.
"Gasoline for the first time is performing better after being beaten up so much in the last two weeks," said Tom Bentz of ING Derivatives.
October heating oil ended up 0.59 cent to 71.49 cents a gallon after falling as low as 69.95 cents as traders took profits from this week's gains, which pushed the market to five-year highs.
Traders said the thin heating oil inventories on both sides of the Atlantic were unusual for this time of year.
"Shortages are usually caused by a sudden cold snap which draws product from one side of the Atlantic to the other to compensate," said Christopher Bellew of London futures brokers Prudential Bache.
But this year, U.S. and European refiners alike have been caught short ahead of winter because of a cost-cutting decision to keep forward supplies to a minimum.

Tensions in the Middle East have provided some support for oil prices in recent weeks, but world oil markets largely shrugged off this week's Israeli-Palestinian violence and saw no immediate threat to Gulf oil supplies.
But some analysts said on Friday that continued bloodshed could scuttle the Midweast peace process and force oil-rich Gulf countries to rethink an already uneasy alliance with the United States.

"This could lead to a medium-term change in attitude of the Arab countries to the U.S. presence there and could undermine the stability of the Gulf," said John Mitchell, chairman of the Energy and Environmentral Programme at the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
November crude ended 44 cents higher at $24.60 a barrrel.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, forecasts for better harvest weather next week pushed prices lower.
December corn ended down 2-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.03-1/4 and November soybeans down 7-1/2 cents at $7.83-1/4.
"The market can't go anywhere because harvest is right around the corner and we're already at historic high (price) levels," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
December wheat closed up 2-1/4 cents a bushel at $4.31-1/2 on ideas that a quarterly government report due on Monday will show stocks below last year's tight supply levels.
Analysts estimated wheat stocks will be reported at 1.767 billion bushels, compared to 1.881 billion a year ago.
Chicago Mercantile Exchange traders said a U.S. Agriculture Department report on the hog population released after the close of trading Friday would fuel buying on Monday.

The government estimated the number of hogs and pigs on farms as of September 1 at 58.2 million animals, or only 96 percent of the herd numbers a year earlier. It also sharply revised down its estimates of the herd last winter.
On Friday October hog futures closed at 57.35 cents per pound, down 0.05 cent, and February pork bellies at 77.575 cents per pound, down 1.675 cents.
